input: An ADCS certificate can remain usable after the template that enabled its issuance has been restored. Investigating that sequence requires evidence from directory changes, certificate issuance and domain authentication, whose records do not always expose matching identifiers. CertGraph combines graph analysis, certificate-specific provenance and remediation under an assigned disruption budget. Its evidence contract scopes certificate identity to the issuer, retains compatible candidates when fields are missing, and revises attribution when later records conflict. We evaluate the contract using synthetic histories and controlled Windows experiments.
actual_output: An ADCS certificate can be used even after the template that permitted its issuance has been restored. Investigating that sequence necessitates evidence from directory modifications, certificate issuance, and domain authentication records, which do not necessarily reveal matching IDs. CertGraph combines graph analysis, certificate-specific provenance, and remediation within a specified disruption budget. Its evidence contract restricts certificate identity to the issuer, keeps compatible candidates when fields are lacking, and revises attribution when subsequent records dispute. We analyze the contract through synthetic histories and controlled Windows experiments.

input: In a frozen 5,400-history study, the randomized subset retains 99.06% of true observed links as candidates and resolves 55.82% definitively. Four intervention matrices and a separate concurrent forest workload provide 72 certificate cases: 66 successful exact-certificate authentications, including 13 administrative uses, and six certificate-bound rejections. Current-patch controls distinguish rejection of UPN-only requests from administrative use of SID-URL certificates after template restoration. A guarded SQLite implementation agrees with the identity reference at all 5,423 evaluated prefixes. Separate graph-learning experiments reproduce 10,800 held-out predictions but find no classification advantage for bilinear gating over matched additive attention.

input: The graph-learning results do not establish a classification advantage for bilinear gating. Both matched literal models miss the tested long-path positives, so a verifier that examines only neural-positive cases remains incomplete for this workload. The remediation experiments likewise show heuristic optimality gaps and budget-dependent differences from greedy selection. Larger deployments require separate measurements of collection cost, retained history and administrator-assigned disruption costs. The present results support these specific conclusions within the recorded laboratory and generator conditions.
actual_output: The graph-learning results do not show a classification advantage for bilinear gating. Both matched literal models miss the tested long-path positives, therefore a verifier that just checks neural-positive situations is insufficient for this workload. The remediation experiments also reveal heuristic optimality gaps and budget-dependent variations from greedy selection. Larger deployments necessitate separate calculations of collecting cost, retained history, and administrator-assigned disruption costs. The current findings corroborate these precise conclusions based on the laboratory and generator settings documented.
